topics.title: Chapter 20 — File Sharing and Network Storage
topics.summary: A local pathname can hide a remote dependency. HarborWorks wants a shared directory for approved reports, but the reports must not become writable by every machine that can reach the server. This chapter connects file sharing to identity, availability, and recovery rather than treating a successful mount as the end of the task.

topics.title: 20.1 Network Filesystems
topics.summary: A network filesystem lets a client access remote files through filesystem operations. The application may use familiar paths while every lookup, read, or write depends on a network and another host. Local-looking behavior does not imply local latency or failure semantics.

blocks.text: A network filesystem lets a client access remote files through filesystem operations. The application may use familiar paths while every lookup, read, or write depends on a network and another host. Local-looking behavior does not imply local latency or failure semantics.

Define the workload before selecting a share. Does it require several writers, locking, stable identity, low latency, encryption, or operation during disconnection? A deployment artifact repository, a user home directory, and a database data directory impose different requirements. Do not put a database on a generic share without the database vendor’s supported storage contract.

Document the server, exported path, client mount point, protocol, security mode, and owner. Test server loss as well as normal operation. A process blocked in a remote filesystem operation may not respond immediately to the signals an operator expects.
Linux example — 20.1
Inspect active network mounts.
findmnt -t nfs,nfs4,cifs
blocks.title: Original Linux example

blocks.text: What to check: No matching mounts may be normal; local filesystem checks do not validate a network server.

topics.title: 20.2 NFS
topics.summary: NFS is a common network filesystem protocol in Unix-like environments. Version and security flavor matter. Establish the negotiated protocol instead of assuming the package name determines it.

An NFSv4 deployment is not operationally identical to an older configuration with additional RPC services and ports. Establish the negotiated protocol instead of assuming the package name determines it.

With traditional AUTH_SYS, client-provided numeric identity is part of the trust model. Restricting access to a subnet does not turn it into strong per-user authentication. For stronger identity and integrity or privacy requirements, evaluate a properly configured Kerberos-based security flavor, such as krb5p, within the organization’s identity infrastructure. (R46)
For the introductory lab, use a read-only export between isolated, administrator-controlled machines. That constrains the exercise without implying it is an enterprise identity design.

nfsstat -m

blocks.text: An export specifies a server directory, allowed clients, and options. On common Linux servers, /etc/exports and included export files define the persistent intent. exportfs -v shows the active interpretation; it is more useful than assuming that an edited file has already taken effect.
An illustrative isolated-network entry is:
/srv/harbor/share 192.168.56.30(ro,sync,root_squash)
blocks.title: Original Linux example

blocks.text: The address must be the verified client, not a guessed network. There must be no space between the client expression and its parenthesized options. ro makes the export read-only. root_squash maps requests claiming client root to an anonymous identity rather than trusting client root as server root. It is not a substitute for securing the client or using stronger authentication.

Apply changes through the supported export-management command after review. Existing clients and services can be affected by export changes, so record the prior active configuration and schedule shared changes deliberately.
Linux example — 20.3
On the NFS lab server, list active exports.
sudo exportfs -v
blocks.title: Original Linux example

blocks.text: What to check: Review client scope, read/write mode, and root squashing before permitting access.
Read-only NFS export candidate
/srv/harbor/reports 192.168.56.0/24(ro,sync,root_squash,no_subtree_check)
blocks.title: Original Linux example

blocks.text: This exports the lab reports directory to the specified lab subnet only. Review ownership, server/client versions, firewall scope, and distribution configuration paths before applying it.

blocks.text: These observations help establish the actual mounts and options. Verify file access as the intended user, not only as root. A mount that root can list may still reject application access because identity or directory permissions differ.

Avoid changing from the default hard-retry behavior to a soft mount merely to stop a process from waiting. Soft timeout behavior can expose applications to I/O errors and data-integrity risks they were not designed to handle. Select options from workload requirements and current protocol documentation, not impatience during an outage. (R46)

blocks.text: Samba provides SMB services on Linux and can participate in several identity roles. A simple standalone share, a domain member, and a domain controller are different designs. This chapter’s example is a standalone file-sharing lab, not instructions for replacing an organization’s identity service.

Samba access depends on both its share policy and the underlying filesystem. Granting access in smb.conf does not bypass Unix permissions or mandatory access control. Conversely, permissive filesystem modes do not necessarily grant access through the share.

Validate a candidate configuration with testparm and inspect the service names supplied by the distribution. On common systems they differ between families. Keep protocol security and supported defaults under review; do not re-enable obsolete SMB versions to accommodate an unexplained client failure. (R47)

Validate Samba configuration.
testparm -s

    read only = yes
    guest ok = no
    valid users = LAB_SMB_USER

    read only = yes
    guest ok = no

blocks.text: Replace LAB_SMB_USER with the approved lab Samba identity, configure its authentication deliberately, and validate with testparm before reloading. The underlying directory permissions must also permit the intended reads.

blocks.text: SMB is the protocol family; CIFS is a historical name still present in Linux mount tooling such as mount.cifs. A command containing cifs does not by itself identify the negotiated SMB dialect. Inspect the client’s capabilities and the server’s effective policy.

Credentials supplied directly in a shell command can leak into history or process inspection. A root-owned, mode-0600 credentials file is safer for a narrow lab, while production should use an approved credential-management and authentication design. Protect that file in backup and configuration management as a secret.

Do not confuse client display mappings such as uid= with changing the server’s authorization decisions. Depending on negotiated Unix extensions and server configuration, ownership presentation can differ from server-side identity. Test permitted reads, writes, creates, renames, and deletes through the actual client application.
Linux example — 20.6
Inspect SMB/CIFS mounts without exposing credentials.
findmnt -t cifs -o TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE
blocks.title: Original Linux example

blocks.text: What to check: Keep credentials in protected files; do not paste secrets into mount command arguments.
SMB mount syntax

# Syntax only; use the verified lab server, share, empty mountpoint, and protected credentials file.
# sudo mount -t cifs //LAB_SERVER/linux-book-reports /mnt/LAB_SHARE \
#   -o credentials=/path/to/PROTECTED_LAB_CREDENTIALS,ro
blocks.code:
# Syntax only; use the verified lab server, share, empty mountpoint, and protected credentials file.
# sudo mount -t cifs //LAB_SERVER/linux-book-reports /mnt/LAB_SHARE \
#   -o credentials=/path/to/PROTECTED_LAB_CREDENTIALS,ro
blocks.title: Original Linux example

blocks.text: Never put the password in the command. Use the version and security settings supported by your reviewed server/client combination and unmount deliberately after the lab.

topics.title: 20.7 Automounting
topics.summary: Automounting activates a mount when its path is accessed rather than necessarily establishing it during boot. This can reduce boot dependencies for optional shares and release idle mounts. It does not make an unavailable server available, nor does it remove application delays on first access.

blocks.text: Automounting activates a mount when its path is accessed rather than necessarily establishing it during boot. This can reduce boot dependencies for optional shares and release idle mounts. It does not make an unavailable server available, nor does it remove application delays on first access.

An automount path should have a clear owner and purpose. Avoid ordinary tools that recursively traverse every mount while diagnosing an unrelated local problem. Such commands can trigger remote mounts or wait on failed servers.

systemd can create automount units from suitable /etc/fstab options, while autofs offers map-based management. Choose one manager for a particular mount point. Two managers trying to control the same directory create confusing ownership of state.
Linux example — 20.7
Inspect systemd automount units.
systemctl list-units --type=automount --all --no-pager

topics.title: 20.8 autofs
topics.summary: autofs uses a master map to associate mount locations with subordinate maps. An indirect map places named shares under a managed parent; a direct map specifies complete mount points. Exact configuration paths and defaults depend on packaging.

blocks.text: autofs uses a master map to associate mount locations with subordinate maps. An indirect map places named shares under a managed parent; a direct map specifies complete mount points. Exact configuration paths and defaults depend on packaging.

For example, a reviewed indirect map might associate /shares with /etc/auto.harbor; that file could name a reports key pointing to the approved server export. This is a relationship to design, not a universal configuration to paste over an existing master map.

After validation and service activation, access the specific path, inspect findmnt, and test idle expiry without leaving shells inside the mounted directory. Record how to diagnose map lookup failures separately from NFS authentication, server availability, and file permission failures. (R48)
Linux example — 20.8
Inspect autofs without triggering a new mount.

systemctl status autofs.service --no-pager
sudo automount -m
blocks.title: Original Linux example

blocks.text: What to check: Requires autofs; review map output before using a path that invokes a remote mount.
autofs map candidates

# Candidate /etc/auto.master.d/linux-book.autofs entry:
/mnt/linux-book /etc/auto.linux-book --timeout=60

# Candidate /etc/auto.linux-book entry:
reports -fstype=nfs,ro web1:/srv/harbor/reports
blocks.code:

blocks.title: Original Linux example

blocks.text: Both files are candidates for the isolated lab. The server and export must already be reachable; inspect automount -m and check source permissions before testing a path.

A failure at any layer can appear to an application as denied access. Identify which layer rejected the operation before expanding privileges.

Numeric UID and GID consistency is especially important for traditional Unix identity sharing. A user called analyst with UID 1100 on one host is not automatically the same identity as analyst with UID 1500 on another. Central identity and tested mapping prevent local naming conventions from becoming an accidental access policy.

For a writeable team share, test inheritance and the lifecycle of a file: creation, editing by another approved user, rename, and removal. Directory permissions control some operations that file modes do not. Never use chmod -R 777 as a substitute for identifying the intended collaborators.

Central identity and tested mapping prevent local naming conventions from becoming an accidental access policy.

For a writeable team share, test inheritance and the lifecycle of a file: creation, editing by another approved user, rename, and removal. Directory permissions control some operations that file modes do not. Never use chmod -R 777 as a substitute for identifying the intended collaborators.
Linux example — 20.9
Compare user IDs with path permissions.
What to check: Numeric IDs and server policy may affect access even when local group names look familiar.

Remounting may be part of recovery after clients are safely quiesced, but preserve evidence and understand active applications first.
